notes.front: For Advanced Security licensing, what is an active committer?
notes.back: Anyone licensed with your organisation or enterprise (not only members) who had a commit pushed to an enabled repository in the last 90 days.
notes.explanation: Each active committer to at least one repository with an Advanced Security feature enabled uses one licence.
notes.example: Like a library that charges for readers who borrowed a book in the last 90 days: signing up alone costs nothing, recent use does.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: Each **active committer** to at least one repository with an Advanced Security feature enabled uses **one license**. A committer is considered active if one of their commits has been pushed to the repository within the last 90 days, regardless of when it was originally authored.

notes.front: In Advanced Security licensing, what does the number of unique committers count?
notes.back: Active committers who contributed only to one repository, or only to repositories in one organisation.
notes.explanation: It is the number of licences you can free by disabling Secret Protection or Code Security for that repository or organisation.
notes.example: Like counting the staff who work only in one branch office: close that office and only those staff stop needing a desk; people who also work elsewhere still need one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: **Unique committers** is the number of active committers who contributed only to one repository, or only to repositories in one organization. You can free up this number of licenses by disabling GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Code Security for that repository or organization.

notes.front: What is metered billing for Advanced Security?
notes.back: A monthly bill for the licences your active committers use, with no pre-defined licence limit and no overage state.
notes.explanation: You pay only for what you use, and you can enable Secret Protection or Code Security independently.
notes.example: Like a pay-as-you-go electricity meter: no fixed allowance to run out of, just a bill each month for what was used.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: * Users can enable GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Code Security independently. * Monthly bill for the number of licenses used by active committers. * No pre-defined license limit. * No overage state, you pay only for what you use.

notes.front: What is volume/subscription billing for Advanced Security?
notes.back: Buying a specific number of licences that last for a defined period, typically at least a year; for GitHub Enterprise plans only.
notes.explanation: The number bought is a limit: usage above it needs additional licences.
notes.example: Like buying a block of 100 season tickets for a year: the 101st person needs another ticket bought.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: **Volume/subscription billing** available for GitHub Enterprise plans only * Purchase a specific number of GitHub Secret Protection, GitHub Code Security, or GitHub Advanced Security licenses that last for a defined period, typically at least a year,

notes.front: Advanced Security is sold as how many licence products (stock keeping units), and what are they?
notes.back: Two: GitHub Secret Protection and GitHub Code Security.
notes.explanation: Under metered billing you can even enable either one independently.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Licenses for GitHub Advanced Security”
notes.evidence: The Advanced Security product has two license SKUs (stock keeping units): * **GitHub Secret Protection**,

notes.front: A committer is considered active if one of their commits has been pushed to the repository within the last {{c1::90 days}}, regardless of when it was originally authored.
notes.explanation: The push date, not the authoring date, is what starts the 90 days.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: A committer is considered active if one of their commits has been pushed to the repository within the last 90 days, regardless of when it was originally authored.

notes.front: Besides organisation members, which people can count as active committers?
notes.back: Enterprise-managed users, external collaborators, and people with a pending invitation to join.
notes.explanation: All of them hold a GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise licence with your organisation or enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: That is, they are also a member, an enterprise-managed user, an external collaborator, or have a pending invitation to join your organization or enterprise.

notes.front: Do GitHub App bots use Advanced Security licences?
notes.back: No. GitHub App bots are ignored when licence usage is calculated.
notes.explanation: Licence usage counts unique, active committers, and bots made by GitHub Apps are left out of that count.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “How usage of GitHub Advanced Security licenses is measured”
notes.evidence: Your license usage is calculated based on the number of **unique, active committers** to repositories with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Code Security features enabled. GitHub App bots are ignored.

notes.front: Usage is measured across the whole organisation or enterprise so that each member uses {{c1::one licence}}, however many repositories or organisations they contribute to.
notes.explanation: Contributing to more enabled repositories does not multiply a person’s cost.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Understanding usage”
notes.evidence: Usage is measured across the whole organization or enterprise to ensure that each member uses one license regardless of how many repositories or organizations the user contributes to.

notes.front: Your unique, active committers exceed your licence limit. What happens on repositories where the products are already enabled?
notes.back: The features keep working there.
notes.explanation: The limit stops you growing, not what you already have.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Using more than your planned licenses”
notes.evidence: If your number of unique, active committers exceeds your license limit, features controlled by Advanced Security licensing continue to work on all repositories where they are already enabled.

notes.front: Over your licence limit, what can you no longer do, and what happens to new repositories set to enable the products automatically?
notes.back: You cannot enable the products on any additional repositories; new repositories are created with the products disabled.
notes.explanation: Blocking new enablement is how the limit is enforced, since existing enablement keeps working.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Using more than your planned licenses”
notes.evidence: However, you will not be able to enable GitHub Secret Protection, GitHub Code Security, or GitHub Advanced Security on any additional repositories. Any new repositories created in organizations where GitHub Secret Protection, GitHub Code Security, or GitHub Advanced Security are configured to be enabled automatically will be created with the products disabled.

notes.front: Where is metered billing available for Advanced Security?
notes.back: On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and on GitHub Enterprise Server from 3.13 onward with GitHub Connect.
notes.explanation: Metered use on the server is billed through the linked enterprise account on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: **Metered billing** available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud and from GitHub Enterprise Server 3.13 onward with GitHub Connect

notes.front: On GitHub Enterprise Server, how is metered use of Advanced Security billed?
notes.back: Through the linked enterprise account on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.explanation: Metered billing on the server is available from version 3.13 onward with GitHub Connect.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: On GitHub Enterprise Server, metered use of Advanced Security products is billed through the linked enterprise account on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

notes.front: Under volume/subscription billing, what must you do if active committers exceed the licences you bought?
notes.back: Purchase additional licences to cover the overage.
notes.explanation: Unlike metered billing, the number bought is a ceiling.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: If the usage of Advanced Security by active committers exceeds the number of licenses purchased, you need to purchase additional licenses to cover this overage usage.

notes.front: Which billing model do all standalone instances of GitHub Enterprise Server use?
notes.back: Volume/subscription licences.
notes.explanation: To change the licence you contact GitHub’s Sales team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Volume/subscription billing”
notes.evidence: All standalone instances of GitHub Enterprise Server use volume/subscription licenses. Contact [GitHub's Sales team](https://enterprise.github.com/contact) if you want to make changes to your license.

notes.front: Under volume/subscription billing, how soon is a user’s licence freed after you remove them from your organisation?
notes.back: Within 24 hours.
notes.explanation: Under volume billing each active committer consumes one licence, so removing a user releases theirs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Volume/subscription billing”
notes.evidence: When you remove a user from your organization account, the user's license is freed within 24 hours.

notes.front: A metered Advanced Security budget uses “Limit usage when budget limit is reached”. What does reaching the limit do?
notes.back: It prevents new enablement; it does not disable Advanced Security where it is already active.
notes.explanation: These budgets are set per product, for Secret Protection and Code Security separately.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Hard budgets for GitHub Advanced Security SKUs”
notes.evidence: For Advanced Security, this option prevents new enablement. It does **not** disable Advanced Security on repositories where it is already active.

notes.front: After a hard budget’s limit is reached, are active committers in already-enabled repositories still billed, and when can you enable more repositories?
notes.back: Yes, they are still counted and billed; more repositories only once the budget is increased or a new billing cycle begins.
notes.explanation: The budget stops new enablement, not billing for what is already on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Hard budgets for GitHub Advanced Security SKUs”
notes.evidence: * Repositories where Advanced Security is already enabled continue to function normally. Active committers in those repositories are still counted and billed. * Advanced Security cannot be enabled on any additional repositories until the budget is increased or a new billing cycle begins.

notes.front: What are the two ways usage can exceed a hard Advanced Security budget?
notes.back: A new committer becomes active in an already-enabled repository; or enabling succeeds on a repository with more committers than the budget has left.
notes.explanation: In both cases you are billed for the usage beyond the limit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Hard budgets for GitHub Advanced Security SKUs”
notes.evidence: * A new committer becomes active in a repository where Advanced Security is already enabled. You are billed for the additional license cost. * When you enable Advanced Security on a repository with more active committers than the remaining budget allows, the enablement succeeds but you are billed for any usage beyond the budget limit.

notes.front: After a repository is migrated with GitHub Enterprise Importer, which contributions consume Advanced Security licences?
notes.back: Only commits and pushes made after the migration.
notes.explanation: Historic contributions from before the migration are not considered.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: When a repository is migrated to GitHub using GitHub Enterprise Importer, GitHub Advanced Security only consumes licenses for commits and pushes made *after* migration.

notes.front: Where in an organisation’s settings do you see current Advanced Security licence usage?
notes.back: Settings → Advanced Security → Configurations → Repositories tab, in the “Apply configurations” section.
notes.explanation: With a volume/subscription licence, the number of licences available is reported there too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing your paid use of Advanced Security”, “Understanding your license usage”
notes.evidence: 3. In the "Security" section of the sidebar, select the **codescan Advanced Security** dropdown menu, then click **Configurations**. 4. Click the **Repositories** tab. 5. In the "Apply configurations" section, your current license usage will be displayed.

notes.front: What is the simplest way to turn off all Secret Protection or Code Security features for some repositories?
notes.back: Create a security configuration with the product disabled at the top level, and apply it to those repositories.
notes.explanation: GitHub advises a very clear name for it, such as “No Code Security”, to avoid confusion.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing your paid use of Advanced Security”, “Turning off Secret Protection or Code Security”
notes.evidence: The simplest way to turn off all Secret Protection or Code Security features for one or more repositories is to create a security configuration where the product is disabled at the top level. You can apply this custom configuration to repositories where you want to turn off paid features.

notes.front: What does the enterprise “Disable Advanced Security” option do?
notes.back: Disables it in all private and internal repositories, sets a policy preventing future paid adoption, and stops billing for future use (metered only).
notes.explanation: It suits metered users who want Advanced Security off and not re-enabled without explicit approval.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Disabling GitHub Advanced Security in an enterprise”
notes.evidence: The **Disable Advanced Security** option: * Disables GitHub Advanced Security in all private and internal repositories * Sets a policy to prevent future paid adoption * Stops billing for future usage (metered billing only)

notes.front: In GitHub’s example timeline, the products are disabled on repository X on 16 August. What does the count become, and until when is X still billed?
notes.back: 20 committers from the next cycle; X is billed until the end of the monthly billing cycle.
notes.explanation: The 20 are repository Y’s contributors; the committers who worked only on X stop counting.

notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Example showing how the active committer count changes over time”
notes.evidence: Billing for repository **X** continues until the end of the monthly billing cycle, but the overall billing count decreases to 20 committers for the next cycle.

notes.front: A developer commits to six enabled repositories across two organisations in the same enterprise. How many Advanced Security licences does she use?
notes.choices:
A) Two, one per organisation
B) One
C) Six, one per repository
D) None, because she contributes to more than one organisation
notes.back: B) One
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: usage is measured across the whole enterprise, so the count does not multiply. D: contributing widely does not remove her from the count.
notes.explanation: Each member uses one licence however many repositories or organisations they contribute to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Understanding usage”
notes.evidence: Usage is measured across the whole organization or enterprise to ensure that each member uses one license regardless of how many repositories or organizations the user contributes to.

notes.front: A contractor authored a commit two years ago on a local branch and pushes it today to a repository with Code Security. Does he now count as an active committer?
notes.choices:
A) No, the commit is older than 90 days
B) Only if he authors a new commit
C) No, contractors never count
D) Yes, because the push happened within the last 90 days
notes.back: D) Yes, because the push happened within the last 90 days
notes.choicesExplained: A: the authoring date does not matter. B: a pushed commit is enough, whenever it was written. C: external collaborators with a licence can count.
notes.explanation: Activity is measured from when the commit is pushed, regardless of when it was authored.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: A committer is considered active if one of their commits has been pushed to the repository within the last 90 days, regardless of when it was originally authored.

notes.front: A GitHub App bot pushes hundreds of commits a week to a repository with Secret Protection. How many licences does the bot use?
notes.choices:
A) None
B) One
C) One per organisation it pushes to
D) One per 90 days of activity
notes.back: A) None
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: GitHub App bots are left out of licence usage entirely.
notes.explanation: Licence usage counts unique, active committers, and GitHub App bots are ignored.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “How usage of GitHub Advanced Security licenses is measured”
notes.evidence: GitHub App bots are ignored.

notes.front: An organisation disables Code Security on one repository with 12 active committers. Four of them commit only there; eight also commit to other enabled repositories. How many licences are freed?
notes.choices:
A) Twelve
B) Eight
C) Four
D) None, until the next year
notes.back: C) Four
notes.choicesExplained: A: the eight who work elsewhere still need their licences. B: those are the ones who stay licensed. D: disabling frees the unique committers’ licences.
notes.explanation: Disabling a repository frees only its unique committers, those who contributed only there.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: **Unique committers** is the number of active committers who contributed only to one repository, or only to repositories in one organization. You can free up this number of licenses by disabling GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Code Security for that repository or organization.

notes.front: An enterprise on volume/subscription billing has gone over its licence count. Its organisations enable the products automatically on new repositories. A team creates a repository today. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) The repository is created with the products enabled and billed as overage
B) All repositories lose Advanced Security until licences are bought
C) Creating the repository fails
D) The repository is created with the products disabled
notes.back: D) The repository is created with the products disabled
notes.choicesExplained: A: over the limit, automatic enablement is skipped. C: the repository is still created. B: existing enablement keeps working.
notes.explanation: Over the limit, no new enablement happens, so automatic enablement is skipped for new repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Using more than your planned licenses”
notes.evidence: Any new repositories created in organizations where GitHub Secret Protection, GitHub Code Security, or GitHub Advanced Security are configured to be enabled automatically will be created with the products disabled.

notes.front: A metered Secret Protection budget with “Limit usage when budget limit is reached” hits its limit mid-month. What happens to secret scanning in repositories that already had it?
notes.choices:
A) It keeps working, and their active committers are still billed
B) It becomes read-only
C) It stops until next month
D) It keeps working free of charge
notes.back: A) It keeps working, and their active committers are still billed
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: the option does not disable Advanced Security where it is active. D: those committers are still counted and billed.
notes.explanation: For Advanced Security the budget option only prevents new enablement.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Hard budgets for GitHub Advanced Security SKUs”
notes.evidence: Repositories where Advanced Security is already enabled continue to function normally. Active committers in those repositories are still counted and billed.

notes.front: A company on GitHub Enterprise Cloud wants Secret Protection only, a monthly bill for actual use, and no fixed licence count to run out of. Which way of paying fits?
notes.choices:
A) Volume/subscription billing
B) A standalone GitHub Enterprise Server licence
C) Metered billing
D) Buying one licence per repository
notes.back: C) Metered billing
notes.choicesExplained: A: it sets a fixed number of licences for a period. B: standalone servers use volume/subscription licences. D: licences are counted per active committer, not per repository.
notes.explanation: Metered billing has no pre-defined limit, bills monthly, and lets you enable either product on its own.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: * Users can enable GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Code Security independently. * Monthly bill for the number of licenses used by active committers. * No pre-defined license limit.

notes.front: A bank runs a standalone GitHub Enterprise Server with no connection to GitHub Enterprise Cloud and wants Code Security. How will it pay?
notes.choices:
A) Volume/subscription licences
B) Metered billing through GitHub Connect
C) Free, as the server is private
D) Per scan
notes.back: A) Volume/subscription licences
notes.choicesExplained: B: metered billing on the server needs GitHub Connect and a linked cloud account. C: every repository on the server needs paid Advanced Security. D: licences are per active committer.
notes.explanation: Metered billing on the server needs GitHub Connect and bills through a linked cloud enterprise account, which a standalone instance does not have.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Volume/subscription billing”
notes.evidence: All standalone instances of GitHub Enterprise Server use volume/subscription licenses.

notes.front: A repository with Code Security gets pushes from four accounts in the last 90 days. Which one uses no licence?
notes.choices:
A) An external collaborator on the organisation’s licence
B) A person with a pending invitation to the organisation
C) A GitHub App bot
D) An enterprise-managed user
notes.back: C) A GitHub App bot
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: each is listed among those who count as active committers.
notes.explanation: Members, managed users, external collaborators and pending invitees count; GitHub App bots are ignored.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: That is, they are also a member, an enterprise-managed user, an external collaborator, or have a pending invitation to join your organization or enterprise.

notes.front: A finance lead asks how many Advanced Security licences one organisation is using right now. Where should its owner look?
notes.choices:

B) The repository’s Security and quality tab

notes.front: An organisation wants to stop paying for Code Security on 40 low-risk repositories but keep Secret Protection there. What is the simplest approach?
notes.choices:
A) Remove every committer from the organisation
B) Delete the repositories’ workflows
C) Apply a custom security configuration with Code Security disabled at the top level
D) Make the repositories internal
notes.back: C) Apply a custom security configuration with Code Security disabled at the top level
notes.choicesExplained: B: workflows do not decide licence use. A: that frees licences but removes the people. D: internal repositories still need the product.
notes.explanation: A security configuration with the product disabled at the top level turns off its paid features wherever you apply it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing your paid use of Advanced Security”, “Turning off Secret Protection or Code Security”
notes.evidence: The simplest way to turn off all Secret Protection or Code Security features for one or more repositories is to create a security configuration where the product is disabled at the top level.

notes.front: Contrast metered and volume/subscription billing: is there a licence limit, and what happens when usage grows?
notes.back: Metered: no pre-defined limit, you pay monthly for what you use. Volume: a set number for a period; overage needs more licences.
notes.explanation: Metered billing has no overage state, while volume billing has a ceiling to buy past.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Paying for GitHub Advanced Security licenses”
notes.evidence: * No pre-defined license limit. * No overage state, you pay only for what you use.

notes.front: Contrast active committers and unique committers: what does each number tell you?
notes.back: Active: the licences in use. Unique: the licences you would free by disabling a repository or organisation.
notes.explanation: Every active committer uses a licence, but only those confined to one repository or organisation are released when it is disabled.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Advanced Security license billing”, “Active and unique committers”
notes.evidence: Each **active committer** to at least one repository with an Advanced Security feature enabled uses **one license**.
